title: How Down Syndrome Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Down syndrome, recorded during Down Syndrome Awareness Month. They cover the caveat that people with Down syndrome vary widely, typical physical traits and associated medical issues, the genetics of trisomy 21 (including translocation and mosaic forms), the history of institutionalization and the term "mongoloid" (including John Langdon Down and Blumenbach's racial classification), deinstitutionalization and rising life expectancy, developmental milestones and occupational therapy, education laws (IDEA and ADA), prenatal screening and testing and the abortion debate, costs and aging, Alzheimer's risk and exclusion from drug trials, a study of self-perception among people with Down syndrome, and a few notable people with Down syndrome. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about a fundamentalism follow-up.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening and framing
segments.summary: Hosts note the episode is recorded in Down Syndrome Awareness Month, discuss how views and health outcomes have changed since the 1970s, and caveat that people with Down syndrome are diverse individuals, not a stereotype.

segments.title: Physical traits and medical issues
segments.summary: Typical physical characteristics such as almond-shaped eyes, a single palmar crease, and small pinky fingers are described, along with low muscle tone, speech delays caused by motor issues, and common medical problems including heart defects, vision and hearing problems, thyroid issues, and early Alzheimer's.

segments.title: Maternal age and risk
segments.summary: The hosts explain how the risk of having a baby with Down syndrome rises with maternal age, roughly 1 in 1,250 at age 25 and about 1 in 100 at 40 and older, averaging about 1 in 700 to 800 births overall.

segments.title: Trisomy 21 genetics
segments.summary: Trisomy 21 is explained as an extra copy of chromosome 21, most often from the mother's egg, with cohesin-type protein degradation as a suspected cause. Chromosome 21 is described as encoding a few hundred genes. Translocation and mosaic forms are covered, along with how mosaic Down syndrome can explain some identical twin discordance.

segments.title: Early history and ancient depictions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss historical depictions of people with Down syndrome, including a clay sculpture and a Flemish painting, and note that people with Down syndrome historically had very short lifespans and were often institutionalized and cast out.

segments.title: Naming and the term mongoloid
segments.summary: John Langdon Down, who described the condition in 1862, gave it his name. The hosts discuss the outdated term mongoloid, Blumenbach's racial classification, the World Health Organization request in 1960, and why the name is written with a capital D and lowercase s. Devo's song Mongoloid and the Black Eyed Peas re-recording are mentioned.

segments.title: Institutionalization and deinstitutionalization
segments.summary: The hosts describe the mistreatment of people with Down syndrome in institutions, and the shift in the 1960s and 1970s toward raising them at home. Life expectancy rose significantly, and a study found higher IQ in home-raised children. Benjamin Spock's 1950s-era advice to institutionalize babies is cited.

segments.title: Development, occupational therapy and education
segments.summary: Developmental differences are covered, including feeding, growth, and speech milestones, and the role of occupational therapy with fine and gross motor skills. Visual learning strengths, integrated classrooms, and federal laws IDEA and ADA are discussed.
